- The first experiment resulted in very similar NLL values for the top 16 models (ranging from -20.45 to -19.61). This indicates that a standard condition (S=1.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0) cannot distinguish between simple Michaelis-Menten, substrate/product deactivation, or higher-order substrate mechanisms. They can all fit the baseline curve by adjusting their respective rate constants.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved. Now we must perturb the system with higher substrate and initial product concentrations to break the degeneracy and separate the leading clusters.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
- Hypothesis discrimination: We need to separate product-induced deactivation (M12, M17), substrate-induced deactivation (M11, M16), higher-order substrate mechanisms (M7), and simple reversible mechanisms (M1). 
- Discriminative experiment design: By setting a high initial product concentration (P=0.5) and an increased substrate concentration (S=2.0) with the same catalyst loading (cat=0.05), we introduce strong competing effects that will trigger the specific deactivation or higher-order pathways of the leading models.
- Contrastive prediction:
  - M17 (P+catS => inactive) and M12 (P+cat => inactive): The presence of P=0.5 from the start will cause immediate and rapid catalyst deactivation, leading to early stalling and very low conversion of the remaining substrate. M17 will deactivate faster than M12 because high S favors the catS state.
  - M7 (S+catS <=> catS2 -> P + catS): Requires two substrate molecules to react. Increasing S to 2.0 will strongly favor catS2 formation, potentially increasing the maximum rate or showing distinct saturation kinetics without premature stalling.
  - M16 (S+catS => inactive) and M11 (S+cat => inactive): The higher S=2.0 will accelerate deactivation compared to Run 1, leading to stalling. However, their initial rates won't be suppressed by P=0.5 as strongly as in M12/M17, allowing us to decouple S-deactivation from P-deactivation.
  - M1 (Simple MM): Will show a normal initial rate (only slightly reduced by reversible P inhibition) and will proceed to thermodynamic equilibrium without permanent catalyst deactivation.
</hypothesis>
